entry.title: Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before
entry.summary: Sandra Wollner's 'Everytime' is filled with the unexpected. She tells IndieWire about video games, that tragic fall, and what it all means. Sort of.
entry.content:
Few human emotions are as fathomable as grief. Someone (or something) was here, had meaning and value and presence, and is now gone. There is a hole, a gap, an empty space. The pain that accompanies that void may manifest in different people in different ways, but its very existence is understandable. What makes people happy? What makes them sad? What makes them angry? Grief, well, that’s an easier question with a tougher answer.

For her third feature film, German filmmaker Sandra Wollner tackles the most tangible of dramatic genres — the grief tale — and turns it on its head in a way that our own David Ehrlich called “infinitely beguiling.” Mostly, the film shows how infinitely elastic and malleable this genre is, and the emotions that power it.

Related Stories
How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies
Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work?

The logline for the Un Certain Regard winner is simple enough: after the death of teenager Jessie (Carla Hüttermann), her mother Ella (Birgit Minichmayr), her little sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling), and her boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) form an unlikely family unit as they attempt to move on. To say much else is spoiler-y in the truest of senses: It would detract from the joy and wonder of watching this story unfold.

That Wollner’s film is doing something different with seemingly well-trod material is obvious from the start, as “Everytime” layers on cut scenes from the video game “Vintage Story” — not “Minecraft,” though Wollner understands why the audience might think it’s the more well-known game — long before the real drama kicks in.

A familiarity with “Vintage Story” is not required to understand her film, Wollner promised during a recent interview with IndieWire. “Maybe if someone hears the dialogue of Melli and Lux, then maybe they would feel they have to know more about it, because they’re talking about how you can basically cut trees to harvest stuff and to get that, but I don’t feel that you have to know anything,” she said.

Wollner herself isn’t even a “hardcore gamer,” but she admires video games for their world-building and how they can encourage exploration. Her early forays into both “Vintage Story” and “Minecraft” tickled that. “It felt like the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon, but before the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon,” she said. “You’re walking through infinite worlds that feel so big, but minimalistic in a way. And the sounds; a very ambient sound feels eerie and soothing at the same time. I was just very compelled and inspired by that.”

The idea that Jessie would leave behind her own video game world that Melli could then play in was one of the film’s first seeds. “I thought, it’s a way of a memorial I haven’t seen so far,” she said. “[We have this] whole world of avatars and gaming communities where people meet online and then if someone really goes out, their avatar might live forever in there and create a life on its own in a way. I just found that very intriguing, and this is why I wanted in there.”

While the film is unique in how it handles digital mementos — avatars, literally — Wollner also pays close attention to real-world details that can make grief feel even bigger.

“One of the first scenes [I thought of] was Ella lying down on the couch and hearing how her daughter would come back [into their apartment],” the filmmaker said. “It’s something I think also everybody can relate to, even with a more natural loss and not such a tragic one. For example, when I was a kid, my aunt would always run down the stairs [in the apartment complex where we lived], and I would always hear her in the morning, running down in the morning. The noise was very specific to this person. I didn’t want it to be full on, but to let us think, it couldn’t be Jessie.”

Wollner was also intrigued early on by the “constellation of people” impacted by the loss of one. “The boy, the little girl, and the mother, it’s people I’ve met in my life in several decades, I would say, variations of them, but somehow similar constellations,” she said. “They seemed very clear to me. Three people who, especially the mother and the boy, really tried to do the right thing in a way. But there is a big conflict in there. They are having a weird dependent relationship. She needs him to grieve. He needs her to forgive. Of course, I could have made this conflict much bigger, but I really was interested in ordinary people who just try to do the right thing and just try to go along with that.”

Having her own child added a new dimension to the film, even for Wollner. The filmmaker was editing the film when her daughter was born (her longtime partner is writer and cinematographer Timm Kröger, who also worked on the digital imaging in “Everytime”), an experience that deepened her understanding of her own work.

In the film’s second half, the trio travel to Tenerife, Spain on holiday, a place that baby Jessie (who we’ve seen in home videos) once visited. There, they discover another baby, who looks just like Jessie, playing happily in the same quiet space that baby Jessie once occupied.

“We watched the scene again of baby Jessie sitting there, and we looked at each other,” she said. “I always understood what [that scene] means for me, but there, we really felt it for the first time, being a parent. And I felt, oh, I really nailed it! I mean, that sounds so stupid, but when I had the baby, I think, as many people feel, you still sometimes have the feeling, oh, where does it come from? It’s suddenly here. Suddenly there’s a person there. It’s like with that moment when she walks around the corner, and baby’s sitting there.”

Wollner was also compelled by the way we memorize different places and the unpredictability of memory. The odd little space, located in the far reaches of the resort’s clubhouse, comes to haunt Ella, Melli, and Lux in different ways, forever linked to Jessie and her absence.

“When my dad died, I was with him, and I suddenly had this image of him standing somewhere in this bend on the river and fishing, and it felt so familiar,” the filmmaker said. “This memory intruded on my present. We cannot control when we get a memory. They’re just coming. Sometimes we can make them happen to come. But we never know if maybe the weird place where we saw our baby sitting or the weird moment is the one that haunts us the most. It’s this weird banal little room with this weird banal kitschy toy that is playing this music. And this is the thing that then comes back.”

Those “banal little” details pack immense emotional power. So do turns from Minichmayr and López, who never turn to over-the-top histrionics to convey their grief. Wollner’s choice to set the majority of the film a year after Jessie’s death helped, giving the characters some distance from the immediate stab of loss.

“It was a conscious choice to pick some time after the death [to mostly focus the film on],” she said. “As a writer, we need to know what happened in the time between, and so I wrote that as well, but it honestly felt not depictable. I feel I can only fail to show that. I wasn’t interested in these big emotions. That just felt too overwhelming. And sometimes we are made to believe that grief comes in these neat boxes to check: Now you’re sad, now you’re angry, now you accept. Maybe you can be angry again, then you accept. It’s just this messy thing that you can feel for a very long time.”

Keiling also offers a nuanced performance, built more on a kid’s curiosity than on saddling the young actress with big, showy scenes. There’s no screaming and crying here, no sobbing or yelling. But that doesn’t mean that Keiling wasn’t accessing some major emotions.

“I love to work with kids,” Wollner said. “And even having a kid, I think I still am a kid in a way. For this one, I met Lotte, I had not met another kid, I only met her, I did not do any other castings. I just fell in love and thought, oh, she’s exactly what I thought of Melli could be and even better, so I trusted the script to her.”

Wollner worked with fellow filmmaker Juli Neuhaus, who served as a “kids’ coach” for the younger members of the cast. Wollner and Neuhaus were eager to meet Keiling where she was. The young performer loves to draw, so she would draw the scenes before performing them, to better understand what they were about, which allowed her to access a full spectrum of feeling.

“With Melli, there was no scene where she really had to act her grief,” she said. “I always felt that the film itself, the editing and the framing, the absence, we see her doing her homework, and then we see the same room behind her, but now we know that the sister is not there anymore, I always felt that this will tell us the grief, so she doesn’t need to act it. If she holds her phone and is texting her sister, it will already make us feel the grief. She doesn’t need to feel the heavy weight of that. So, actually for her, it was, I would say, like a very light shoot. Playful. It was really playful.”

Still, for all its sense of fantasy and play, “Everytime” is about a terrible heartbreak. Yet, as ever, Wollner chose to depict Jessie’s sudden, shocking death in a unique way, tracking her fall from a tall building while out with Lux from a great distance away. We can see it. We can do nothing about it. That’s grief, too.

“This was one that really was clear to me in the writing process already, that we’re going to have this lens and that we have this weird perspective of the universe itself looking at it, being so far away and still not able to do something about it, but still witnessing so intimate,” she said.

The actors were on one high-rise building, while Wollner and her crew were on another, about half a mile away. “And we had this insane lens. I had a 3,000-millimeter consumer camera, which is an insane lens,” she said. “It’s really like you don’t want to point it on people. It feels really not OK. But I was sure that I wanted to work with exactly that length or something similar to that, that feels kind of forbidden to be so close and too far away at the same time.”

While the scene is shot as if Jessie and Lux are very close to the edge of the building, the actors were not. (Hüttermann later told Wollner that she still had the feeling she might fall, even with myriad safety measures in place. That’s just how immersive the entire thing felt.) Hüttermann’s actual fall was shot in a studio, and their visual effects supervisor Kariem Saleh combined that footage with the outdoor shots.

Because they needed a certain kind of light, Wollner estimated they had only about five takes to get it right, though she knew they would likely only get one shot with the “perfect” light. Her script also called for the camera to follow a bird after the fall, but she said with a laugh, “Unfortunately, no bird came in exactly that moment.” (They lensed other birds, though, and those also ended up in the final composite shot.)

“We worked so many hours just on the sounds, just to get the right level of there is a little sound, and there is a little tink when she falls down, a little bit,” she said. “Just to realize, given how far away we had to be, how does the sound have to be? We worked the whole time on that, and I never really felt it until I sat at Cannes in the audience. And I heard the gasps for the first time and really it went through my bones. I mean, it’s weird to say that, but I was happy, but I felt the first time that it actually worked.”

Wollner remains very emotionally connected to the film, constantly talking about the way certain scenes make her feel, either while making them or editing them or even seeing them with an audience. Of course, such a deep-feeling filmmaker crafted such a beguiling film, one that invites all sorts of responses and theories. Since Cannes, audiences have been talking about its genuinely thrilling third act and the implications of its final scenes. And while we won’t spoil them here, we had to ask: What did Wollner want her viewers to feel in those moments?

“The feeling that I wanted to have is that [this film that is] grounded or hopefully grounded in the beginning, then suddenly you walk around the corner and you feel still some ground, but it’s such an odd place now and you don’t know,” she said. “I always hoped it doesn’t feel just dreamy, but there is some groundedness to it and that the people still react in a way that made sense for them, the characters, but that you don’t know what room you entered now, some kind of back room. That was clear from the beginning.”

And, as fantastical as it might sound, she’s clear: it’s all real. “I mean, it’s such a cliché to say that, but everything we see at the end is true at the same time,” she said.

A 1-2 Special release, the film is in limited theaters now, with a wide release to come in February 2027.

entry.title: How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies
entry.summary: GKids president Dave Jestead digs into the box office records for "Godzilla Minus Zero," including Imax marketing and demand for foreign language film.
entry.content:
“Godzilla Minus Zero” almost pulled of a Godzilla-times-three on its opening weekend, earning $31.6 million in North America to nearly triple the domestic debut of its 2023 predecessor “Godzilla Minus One.” With that Godzilla math, it destroyed the record for the biggest North American debut for a live-action foreign language film.

It was a crowning moment for the speciality distributor GKIDS. Founded in 2008, the label primarily built itself as a distributor of foreign language animated features, most notably with its acquisition of the North American distribution rights to the Studio Ghibli library. As a day-one employee of GKIDS, and its president since 2017, Dave Jesteadt has helped expand the stateside audience for subtitled features. After a 2025 acquisition by Toho, the Japanese film industry giant behind “Godzilla,” the reach of GKIDS is wider than ever with “Minus Zero,” which drew a box office debut that some studio tentpoles this year would envy.

Related Stories
Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work?
Attend, the First Marketplace Connecting Filmmakers Directly to Theater Owners, Finally Launches Today

“Anecdotally, so many people I know are like, ‘I took my dad this movie and he doesn’t go to any subtitle movies,'” Jesteadt told IndieWire. “Godzilla brings us together. If we’re spreading the gospel of foreign cinema, and Godzilla is a vehicle to get people to engage with great films and deep themes, then I’m all for it.”

After a flashy premiere at the New York Film Festival and a historic cume from IMAX and other premium large-format auditoriums, Jesteadt digs into how GKIDS helped “Minus Zero” come to America.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: “Godzilla Minus One” was seen as a breakout success in 2023, with $57 million in North America. What lessons did GKIDS take away from Toho‘s release of “Minus One” in building toward this big opening for “Minus Zero”?

Dave Jesteadt: GKIDS joined the Toho Group in October 2024, but our story of working together on this began before that, back in 2023. GKIDS had “The Boy and the Heron” from Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli in theaters just a week after “Godzilla Minus One” opened, which was being handled by Toho’s L.A. office at the time. We got to know that team because we had these two films in theaters, sort of competing for similar audience profiles.

In terms of lessons that both sides took, it’s that you can really drive conversation with theaters as a source of celebration and community. When we joined the Toho Group, we took in the team that worked on “Minus One.” We re-released “Shin Godzilla” in 2025 as a test for bringing modern Japanese “Godzilla” films to theaters. Then the planning for “Minus Zero” really began in terms of how we could build and improve on the audience that “Minus One” already found.

Did “Minus Zero” get a bigger marketing spend stateside? How did you consider which people to reach to expand the audience for a Japanese “Godzilla” film?

I can’t give a specific number, but I’d say that we’re very efficient and very mindful of how we can reach the audience in the most direct way possible. For this film, we have the great benefit of our colleagues at Toho International owning and operating Godzilla.com, overseeing merchandise licensing. They have direct communication with the “Godzilla” fan as they exist in America.

But the other goal is to reach, as “Minus One” did, an audience that hadn’t engaged in Japanese “Godzilla” films. We also balanced reaching that core “Godzilla” fan and making sure that they turn out with this desire to continue the story from “Minus One,” reminding people that these films from director Takashi Yamazaki really speak to broader feelings today. They have prestigious bona fides through playing film festivals and great critical reviews. We’re leading with the quality of the film, making people feel that this is a very safe choice — not just if you like spectacle, but that this is going to be one of the best films of the year.

The New York Film Festival premiere played as a flex, especially after a stretch where Hollywood would premiere summer blockbusters at Cannes, draw mediocre reviews, and then have to weather weeks of bad buzz for their expensive tentpoles. With the NYFF premiere, “Minus Zero” was positioned as a prestige object. Is that the aura you were trying to cultivate around it?

I think so. Godzilla has been one of the most famous characters in the world. There’s a big audience that you can potentially address. But the “Minus” franchise takes it into more realistic, human-centered stories. That differentiates it. It is a risk to go to a film festival; I think that has been pretty well-argued. It is a risk anytime you want to share something with the world early before you open, especially when you have such high hopes about how it’s going to go. On the other hand, this was a really important way to demonstrate confidence.

“Minus Zero” opened in more than 3,200 theaters, roughly 1,000 more theaters than “Minus One.” How much did you expand its presence in premium large-format auditoriums?

“Minus Zero” was the first Japanese production filmed for IMAX. That was a central part of the very first announcement and it was a defining part of the marketing campaign. IMAX mentioned it was the highest-indexed opening gross on IMAX screens for an opening weekend in the U.S. We had Godzilla Day on November 3, with IMAX early access screenings globally. So, PLFs definitely played a big presence: Imax, 4DX, Dbox, and others. That’s very unusual for a subtitled foreign film.

It speaks to the expectations for high quality that audiences brought. The PLF story is a way to reinforce production quality. Everyone is saying, “You have to see it in the biggest screen possible with the best sound.” I’ve seen many, many beautiful foreign films. They often end up playing circuits to audiences that are very passionate, but don’t have access to those kind of screens. So it’s a privilege to be able to play a film on the kind of screen that’s typically reserved for the biggest mainstream titles.

How long are you staying in IMAX and PLFs?

It depends on the market. We’re definitely here for the rest of this week. But as “The Odyssey” and other titles have demonstrated, there’s such draw to these moments. It can even create this quest to see something in multiple formats. But as we head into the Thanksgiving frame, the Hollywood competition is obviously huge. We’re realistic about that, even while we’re trying to encourage people to see it as soon and as often as they can.

The reported statistic that more than 70 percent of grosses came from PLFs seems a bit of a double-edged sword to me. It speaks to a high regard for the film among consumers, but it also might indicate that it has a specialized audience that may only want to see the movie in a premium format. Is that a consideration GKIDS takes in, particularly when other titles are taking those auditoriums in the coming weeks?

Obviously, PLFs are time-sensitive. It’s not just about performance, but also about new titles coming in. We’re up against the biggest studios in the world. I’m obviously thrilled that we were able to get so many and I’m thrilled that people saw it that way. I also encourage everyone to just see it in regular theaters too. The way that it was mastered and the way that director Yamazaki made the film is so you won’t have a bad experience in any house watching it. But with any of these core fandoms, there’s a lot of interest in seeing something “the right way.” I’m happy for that, but then the hope is they tell their friends and we continue the growth from there.

You’ve been with GKIDS since its inception and have played a major part in growing the American audience for foreign language cinema. What do you think has changed in the marketplace that has allowed a Japanese “Godzilla” film to now find a much broader audience in the West than it could find before?

There’s no doubt that the quality of the films really helps. “Minus One” was a fantastic film. It won the Oscar for visual effects and became an audience darling. But really, the thing that’s changed the most is that younger generations are much more open to subtitled and foreign cinema than they would have been 10 or 20 years ago. We’ve entered an age of opportunity where what can constitute a hit film is really broadening. That gives me a lot of optimism compared to negative stories about the overall economics of the industry. GKIDS has been bringing subtitled animated movies and anime to audiences for almost 20 years and seeing that audience grow naturally. At first, dubs were essential; now, they’re not.

Though GKIDS isn’t producing these films, I’m curious if, as a distributor, you think that Japanese productions like “Minus Zero” are now being developed and produced with more of a global audience in mind.

The films are still intrinsically Japanese and are basically impossible to separate from the cultural tradition of “Godzilla” in Japan, as well as the overall Japanese film industry. On the other hand, there’s no doubt that the property has the ability to reach a global audience. The popularity with the “Minus” series is really a focus on quality, and how its storytelling is rooted in a time and a place that feels authentically Japanese. Although it deals with a post-war moment in Japanese history, it is incredibly contemporary in terms of the thoughts and preoccupations of a global audience.

So I don’t think there’s necessarily a change in focus. I would say that the audience and the director are in a much more direct conversation. On social media now, everything is auto-translated. You can see real-time active conversation between Japanese fans and viewers commenting about the film with American or Spanish or European audience. Everyone is able to share their thoughts or opinions about some of these themes in a way that brings local perspective to the table. By creating something that feel like it’s created for a specific audience, ironically, you end up making it feel more universal, just because it feels more lived in.

Do you think we are headed to a world where a Japanese “Godzilla” film can outgross a Western “Godzilla” film in North America?

I don’t really think about that. I’m very competitive against a lot of people, but the “Godzilla” franchise has benefited from having a lot of flavors to it. By building that big tent, it ends up being a character that has endured.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now in theaters.

entry.title: Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work?
entry.summary: Democrats won the midterms, but Hollywood crews still await work. How film tax credits, L.A. reforms and Skydance could shape their next paycheck.
entry.content:
Tom Curley is happy about the election results. Whether they’ll help him get back to work is another matter. The production sound mixer, who won an Oscar for “Whiplash,” told IndieWire he has struggled to find consistent employment since his last gig, “CSI: Vegas,” was canceled in 2024.

He’s picked up some work here and there, but nothing has restored the professional footing Curley said he had just two years ago: a loss that has felt “humiliating.”

“I kind of feel like I was in a car accident almost, and I’m just here staring at the aftermath, wondering how I’m going to pick up the pieces, if I’m ever going to pick up the pieces,” he said. “It’s a very destabilizing thing.”

Related Stories
DC Studios’ Latest Reboot: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s Exit Is About Cost-Cutting, Not Just Creative Issues
Attend, the First Marketplace Connecting Filmmakers Directly to Theater Owners, Finally Launches Today

Before last week’s midterms, Curley was cautiously optimistic about a proposed federal tax credit designed to keep more film and TV production work inside the U.S. Now, he’s worried the blue wave could inadvertently slow a bill that had been gaining momentum on both sides.

With Republicans meeting such dramatic electoral losses on November 3, Curley fears President Trump could withdraw his support for the proposed tax credit as a kind of punishment.

“All it takes is some hurt feelings to get in the way,” he said.

But the election was mostly good news for Hollywood, right? Democrats won back both chambers of Congress, and Xavier Becerra (also a Democrat) will soon succeed Gavin Newsom as governor of California — still home to the country’s largest film and TV production workforce.

Meanwhile in LA, Nithya Raman beat incumbent Mayor Karen Bass after explicitly campaigning to make it easier to shoot here. Raman’s victory was widely seen as a rebuke of the status quo in a city where production jobs have become increasingly difficult to find. It’s also part of a broader Democratic promise to make the economy work better for the people who actually depend on it, crews included.

Yet for the scads of film and TV workers IndieWire spoke to in Los Angeles, being pleased with the election results politically didn’t necessarily mean expecting more work to come their way.

Hollywood is a state of mind, sure. But it’s also a literal place where residents have rent due even when the industry isn’t thriving — and inflation, gig-economy restrictions, SAG-AFTRA contract uncertainty, permitting headaches, artificial intelligence, inaccessible healthcare, corporate consolidation, and, yes, productions increasingly leaving town are making the gaps between paychecks harder to survive.

Legislation can help crews in L.A., but Hollywood executives still decide what gets made, where it gets made, and who gets hired in the end. For someone like Curley, even one more gig would help with the bills. The harder question is what comes after that opportunity wraps, and whether today’s labor market can still offer the people who make movie magic enough for a real living.

Can Congress Pass the Federal Film Credit Before 2027?

The first test for this new establishment comes even before the majority takes office.

In the first quarter of 2025, roughly 46 percent of scripted American projects tracked by Luminate were filmed entirely abroad. That’s part of a broader trend toward international production that has drawn bipartisan concern in the U.S. since the late ‘90s.

Right now, Sen. Adam Schiff and Rep. Laura Friedman, both Democrats from California, are trying to pass a federal production tax credit through the outgoing Congress during the lame-duck session. The bill was introduced in September with bipartisan backing — including from South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott and Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran, both Republicans returning to Congress next year.

The proposed Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act would lower the cost of hiring film and TV workers in the U.S. by giving eligible productions a national tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying pay. Bonuses could bring that up to 30 percent, although qualifying projects would generally need to cost over $1 million and spend at least 75 percent of their principal photography days in the U.S.

Some domestic post-production and visual effects work would qualify for federal tax breaks, too, and paired with the right state incentives, film producers could reliably use those savings to motivate new work. In fact, Curley said the people who’d hired him before were explicitly waiting for a federal incentive along those lines. That made the proposal feel like a possible job, not just another bill.

“I’ve been in a survival state of mind for the past couple of years, and I would say my nerves are pretty frayed,” he said. “So I’m extra sensitive to potential downfalls to this whole plan that we’re hoping goes through.”

Still, legislators say there’s cause for hope. Rep. Friedman told IndieWire on November 9 that the House bill had 54 cosponsors, evenly split between Democrats and Republicans.

“I’m working to get this done as soon as possible because film and television workers need these jobs back now, not in a few months or a couple of years,” she said.

With weeks left in the current Congress, attaching the credit to a larger bill already headed for a vote might speed things up. But responding to IndieWire, Friedman didn’t identify a specific legislative package that could carry the measure to a scheduled floor date right now. If the proposal doesn’t become law before this session ends, lawmakers will have to reintroduce the initiative next year.

“It will take both parties working together to get this across the finish line, and we are pushing hard to make this much-needed incentive a reality,” Sen. Schiff told IndieWire in a statement.

Friedman noted that, as written, the credit could possibly take effect as early as January 1 — again, if the bill is signed before 2027. That could establish when production could qualify, but it doesn’t tell us when out-of-work crews might actually start getting calls. What’s more, when those job offers finally do come through? They could be far from old creative hubs like Los Angeles.

What If “Made in America” Still Means Out of Town?

Richard Sanchez has a production job in California right now, and he knows how much that counts.

“I’m one of the very lucky folks who is working at the moment,” the visual effects editor told IndieWire by email. “But admittedly it’s lean and has been lean for quite a while.”

Tax credits have put states in fierce competition for film and TV jobs, from the first day of shooting to the final edit. And in September, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed AB 2319 — specifically creating a separate California tax credit for post-production work. The state is scheduled to start allocating those credits on July 1, 2027, and the yearly budget will ultimately determine how much is available to give out.

“It’s a start, it needs more funding but I hope that brings work in,” Sanchez told IndieWire.

California already makes up to $750 million a year available through its broader film and TV production credit. That previously expanded program began in July 2025 and generally covers 35 percent of qualifying spending, with a higher initial rate for TV series that relocate here. That can help California land a show, but it doesn’t guarantee steady employment for crew members. Studios still decide how many episodes to order and where to send the post-production work.

In the third quarter of 2026, projects in the program accounted for 40.3 percent of scripted on-location filming in Greater Los Angeles (nearly double their share a year earlier), according to FilmLA’s quarterly report. But over the same period, total on-location filming across the region fell 4.8 percent.

“Where the tax credit applies, it’s working to bring productions back to Los Angeles and put local crews to work,” FilmLA CEO Denise Gutches said in a statement to IndieWire. “Still, overall production remains far below where Los Angeles needs it to be, and crews and businesses across the region are feeling it.”

FilmLA also counts shoot days, not jobs or paychecks. So, those figures can’t tell us how many people were hired, how much they made, or whether they worked enough to qualify for benefits. One person who responded to IndieWire’s Reddit callout and identified themselves as a Bay Area camera operator said they were working on a union production but doubted they’d log enough hours for health coverage.

Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra called the current program “the floor” during his campaign and pledged to expand. Newsom’s proposal would raise the annual cap to at least $1 billion, make expenses such as actors’ pay eligible, and set aside $100 million a year for indie productions. Those changes still need legislative approval, but Becerra’s first budget will give crews a better idea of what he’s prepared to seek.

As for Curley, he got a brief stint with the U.S. main unit of “Artificial,” which shot partly in San Francisco, but most of the shoot, he said, took place in Italy. A federal credit might make a U.S. production more attractive to filmmakers facing such a choice, but then there’s the question of which state they’ll choose.

Georgia, for example, offers a 20 percent base credit plus another 10 percentage points for productions that promote the state, with no annual cap on how much productions can earn in credits. California and Georgia count different expenses, so the percentages are only part of the calculation.

And a producer weighing L.A. and Atlanta gets to run the numbers both ways — while a crew member who’s spent years building a career in one city has a different calculation to make. If the next show goes across the country, can they afford to follow it? Can they afford to stay put and wait? Either way, more American projects won’t necessarily mean more openings for the crews Hollywood has left behind.

How Can L.A. Actually Get Cameras Rolling Again?

“We can’t always be the cheapest, so we need to be the easiest.” That’s how Pamala Buzick Kim, a co-founder of the production advocacy group Stay in LA, sees the city’s job supporting the industry.

A tax credit can make a shoot look good on paper. But someone still has to get the permits, pay the fees, and figure out what happens when the next location runs across a city line. Buzick Kim said mayor-elect Nithya Raman’s office regularly talked with Stay in L.A. about what was getting in the way of filming and what the city could practically do about it. Those conversations made her optimistic.

“Everybody’s looking after their small piece of the pie, which is what their job is,” Buzick Kim said. “But we have not instituted any infrastructure to look out for our business in Los Angeles as a whole.”

Raman’s office did not immediately respond to IndieWire’s request for comment. But her campaign platform called for a staffed film office within the mayor’s office, clearer permit timelines, lower fees for smaller productions, and regular reviews of neighborhood filming restrictions. She also pledged to work with the county and neighboring jurisdictions so productions could move more easily.

“If we’re going to incentivize more people to roll here we need to cut down permit processing times, lower fees, and lift unnecessary restrictions on local filmmaking,” echoed film and TV editor Andy Young in an email to IndieWire. Young volunteered for Raman in the primary and worked as a paid freelance video editor for her campaign during the general election. (He said he was speaking for himself.)

“I’m excited to have a Mayor that sees LA as an industry town, sees how bleak things are right now, and has a real sense of urgency when it comes to filling sound stages and getting cameras rolling again,” Young wrote.

Some of Raman’s proposed changes will take cooperation across local groups. For example, FilmLA coordinates applications and charges for its services, but city officials approve permits and set some of the fees that FilmLA ultimately collects. A new administration at City Hall will have to work with the people already making those decisions to successfully enact changes.

Of course, for a smaller shoot, every cost makes a difference. FilmLA and the city recently extended their low-impact permit pilot through April 30, 2027, meaning qualifying productions can apply for just $350, compared with the standard $931 application fee. A few days on a commercial can pay the bills between longer jobs, and Buzick Kim wants city residents to see community when film crews take over their block.

“How do we get residents to be more favorable and optimistic about production?” she asked for Stay in LA. “How do we get them understanding that these are your neighbor’s jobs?”

Curley said he didn’t know enough about permitting to say how much a film office would practically help with the issues he’s been facing. After all, for years, the city’s reputation as the best place in the world for movies “was our film office,” he said. Still, taken together, Curley’s dry spell and the Stay in LA pitch assume that literal Hollywood, like anywhere else, must earn its place amongst national competition.

Where Do Crews Fit Into Skydance’s $6 Billion Savings Plan?

California voters chose new leadership in Washington, the state capital of Sacramento, and LA’s City Hall. But hey didn’t get say on who would own two of Hollywood’s biggest studios.

On October 6, less than a month before the election, Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The deal followed a separate earlier merger in August 2025, when Skydance and Paramount Global combined.

In its November 9 investor update, Skydance said it was aiming for at least $6 billion in annual savings within three years. Those plans include combining back-office functions and using more AI in some corporate workflows. Investors got a number and a deadline, but production crews are still waiting to see how much work the combined company will actually have for them.

An August analysis commissioned by L.A. County estimated that the merger could put about 4,500 local film and TV jobs at risk over the next three years. That was an estimate of potential losses, not a count of people already laid off. It also preceded the fall settlement, which required additional production spending.

California and other states did get some promises in writing from Skydance. A court-approved settlement disclosed in an SEC filing requires the new company to release a minimum number of films in theaters and bars it from selling or closing the Paramount and Warner Bros. studio lots for five years. The deal also requires the company to spend at least $1.5 billion more on U.S. filmmaking over that period than the two companies would have spent at their combined pace in 2025.

But where will that business go? Curley, for one, can imagine some good coming out of an industry that’s scattered beyond Los Angeles. Maybe more people will get a shot at making something of their own. Maybe there’ll be a burst of indie filmmaking like the one he associates with the ’70s.

The Academy Award-winning craftsman can also see doors closing for people who’ve spent their working lives learning how to make movies.

“Maybe this is a good thing for the young people,” he said. “I’m hoping that’s the case anyway.”

It’s an oddly fitting coda for the “Whiplash” production sound mixer, but still not the one he wants. For now, Curley already has an Oscar. What he needs is a call time and the chance to create again.

entry.title: Attend, the First Marketplace Connecting Filmmakers Directly to Theater Owners, Finally Launches Today
entry.summary: AFM: Attend, a theatrical marketplace designed to connect filmmakers directly to theater owners as designed by The Fithian Group, has launched today.
entry.content:
Way back in October 2024, The Fithian Group, led by former NATO chief John Fithian and founding partner Patrick Corcoran, announced plans for an ambitious new marketplace, one that would help connect filmmakers and their projects directly to theater owners looking to book their movies and effectively cut out the distribution middleman. Today, that vision is now a reality.

The Fithian Group on Wednesday at the American Film Market announced the formal launch of Attend Theatrical Marketplace, the group’s online platform and marketplace for filmmakers and exhibitors that is now live and ready for business.

Attend launches with today just a curated selection of four films, all of whose filmmakers will now be doing the legwork to connect with theaters and find venues at which to exhibit their work. But the platform is already loaded with exhibition partners who will be able to browse available films, with more to be added soon, and Attend will eventually be a fully open platform to any filmmaker who wishes to do outreach directly to theater owners.

Related Stories
DC Studios’ Latest Reboot: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s Exit Is About Cost-Cutting, Not Just Creative Issues
‘Paper Tiger’ Review: Adam Driver Gives a Career-Best Performance in James Gray’s Devastating Tragedy

IndieWire got an early demo of Attend and how it aims to simplify the work that distributors do every day in putting movies into theaters, as well as the work exhibitors have to do in booking movies, paying invoices, and more. And IndieWire will on Wednesday lead a panel discussion at AFM with Corcoran, Charles Beale of the site’s designer Titlepool, and filmmaker Lilian T. Mehrel, whose Tribeca award-winning film “Honeyjoon” will be one of the four inaugural films shopping for theaters.

Beyond “Honeyjoon,” the other three films available on Attend at launch are Kenny Riches’ crime drama “Mouse”; “Spoke,” which is a documentary about firefighters and the trauma they deal with after the fires; and “Censurada,” an LGBTQ+ drama from Marco Garza about forbidden love in 1969 Spain.

The vision of Attend was outlined to IndieWire over a year ago with an indie rom-com called “You, Me, and Her” serving as an early guinea pig for the idea. The thinking was, if you had a film that could demonstrate it already had an audience and you had a clear sense of where your audience was and how to target them, all you needed were the screens to showcase your movie and the means to get your movie into the hands of those theaters.

That was and remains the tricky part. Few people have the connections with theater owners to be able to reach them and get a film out in any meaningful capacity. This year has produced a number of examples in which enterprising filmmakers have done without distributors and found the audience they already knew was there to release their movies. YouTuber Markiplier went directly to theaters and made $50 million with his horror movie “Iron Lung.” The documentary “NAZA” skipped a distributor in order to get its story about the IDF out with urgency. Even an AI movie called “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is next month releasing without the aid of a distributor.

Attend seeks to use technology to simplify that process, to get your film out to an even wider audience and a more targeted one. For filmmakers, the platform is designed to eliminate the guesswork of who you need to talk to, how you reach them, and what attributes a given exhibitor is looking for in a film. For exhibitors, it filters all your titles and screens into one place, and it makes the receiving of deliverables or the payment of invoices more automated than the often tedious work it is for most exhibitors today. It’s exciting to see the whole vision come into fruition.

On the filmmaker end, the way Attend works is you as an individual can upload details and assets about your film, from simple details like its runtime, logline, and genre, to much more granular details about the aspect ratio, the available formats, the awards it has won and festivals it has played, the social networking reach of talent, and many more data points. There may be assets you don’t realize will be significant to a given exhibitor but will jump out as they browse your profile. You can then identify themes that speak to the film’s target audience and narrow the demographics for which your film is intended.

From there, you can filter and browse theaters to identify which theaters would be the best fit for your movie. For instance, Attend has data that can show a theater is within walking distance of a firehouse or that the theater has ties to a local advocacy group that aligns with the themes of the film’s story, and Attend’s predictive AI engine can recommend those theaters that would be available and the best fit for your film. Then, instead of reaching out to each of those theaters individually, filmmakers can easily select all the relevant theaters they want to message and have the option to manually add or subtract more beyond the recommended targets. You can even modify proposed theatrical terms for individual theaters or personalize messages, and as theaters come in, Attend can dynamically estimate P&A spend for those locations.

When theater owners are contacted, they’ll receive push notifications about films that are available for them to review, and they can further browse any available films in the marketplace and do their own outreach. Exhibitors can create tabs and info on any number of their circuit’s screens or locations and can upload in spreadsheets specs like screen size, audio, and seat count that filmmakers can view themselves to better get a sense of which theaters are the best fit. Exhibitors can specify rental prices for individual screens, you can mark your theater as being willing to offer simple four-walling options or that it’s capable of hosting big premieres, whether you want to offer “split screens” or “clean screens,” or you can set terms for how long you’re able to hold a movie. And not only does it also itemize marketing costs, Attend clearly indicates what the share of a film’s box office would be if they were to accept it and program it.

This helps theater owners in a number of ways. It takes the busy work out of things like paying numerous individual vendors or distribution partners, and it lets you download and easily generate a W9 form based on that film’s booking, being able to do so across multiple locations. But for theater owners that generally don’t know what they’re playing until the Monday before, this gives theaters far more advanced leeway and awareness to then be able to do the necessary marketing, put tickets on sale, and actually get butts in seats. All that is especially important for the smaller indies that need that word of mouth.

For now, theaters haven’t linked their loyalty data or other point of sales or scheduling tools to Attend, but that could come with time, and as people actually begin to use the platform, the predictive functionality will improve in the long run.

Corcoran and Fithian see Attend being useful for smaller distributors themselves in the long run, not just individual filmmakers who want to cut out the middleman. Distributors can use it to plan the campaigns of multiple titles and use its automation features to save time and costs. And while today Attend just supports new releases, there’s no reason why older library titles couldn’t be marketed here to exhibitors as well.

Time will tell if filmmakers find Attend an effective form of reaching theaters or if exhibitors adopt the platform widely to make it a useful tool for all parties. But it’s an ambitious vision that if implemented properly could have enormous impacts for the independent film world. And after two years of effort and hype, that day could finally be here.

entry.title: DC Studios’ Latest Reboot: James Gunn and Peter Safran’s Exit Is About Cost-Cutting, Not Just Creative Issues
entry.summary: James Gunn and Peter Safran's ouster at DC Studios is about cost-cutting, not just box office.
entry.content:
When they were hired to run DC Studios, James Gunn and Peter Safran were tasked with turning the struggling comic book company into a true rival to Marvel. Four years later, the two have been handed their walking papers before they were able to accomplish their task.

Skydance, which recently bought Warner Bros. Discovery and with it the rights to heroes like Superman, Batman, and the other DC staples that Gunn and Safran were trying to reinvigorate, opted to go in another, cheaper direction. They brought in Jeremy Latcham, a low-profile executive who, like Gunn, had spent years working for Marvel, to oversee DC’s latest reboot.

Related Stories
‘Paper Tiger’ Review: Adam Driver Gives a Career-Best Performance in James Gray’s Devastating Tragedy
‘Iron Boy’ Trailer: Beloved Animated Feature Oscar Contender Throws a Whole Watercolor World Out of Whack

There have been mutterings that the change was because of the commercial performance of DC’s films, and the track record has been a mixed bag. “Superman” did what it needed to do, earning $618.7 million worldwide on a $225 million budget, but it wasn’t a blockbuster on the level of Christopher Nolan’s “Dark Knight” films or “Aquaman.”

But “Supergirl” was an unmitigated disaster, earning $126.5 million against a $170 million budget, resulting in losses of roughly $100 million. And “Clayface,” a body horror film produced for $44 million, has been a modest success, earning approximately $110 million. So no, Gunn and Safran had yet to produce a “Guardians of the Galaxy”-style smash that taps the zeitgeist. Though, to be fair, Marvel hasn’t made as many of those lately either. Tastes have changed, and comic book movies, at least ones not starring Spider-Man, aren’t as popular as they once were.

But look closer, and Gunn and Safran’s ouster is about something more than their films’ commercial performances. It’s about cost-cutting too, something that Skydance, with its $80 billion in net debt, needs to start chipping away at if it’s going to realize the $6 billion in savings it’s promised to find.

The duo’s deal, which was set to expire in 2027, was unusually generous. Safran not only got paid to run the comic book label, he was also allowed to run The Safran Company, the wildly successful production company behind “The Conjuring” franchise (former Netflix film chief Dan Lin, in contrast, divested from his company Rideback when he went over to the streamer). Then there was Gunn, who commanded fees for producing films like “Supergirl” and “Clayface,” as well as fees for those DC films that he wrote and directed, such as “Superman” and “Man of Tomorrow.” Gunn’s total haul for a DC film could be as high as $10 million for all his various duties, according to insiders.

When Warner Bros. Discovery chief David Zaslav offered the pair such a sweet deal, comic book movies looked more durable and he needed to make a splash after DC produced flops like “Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom” and “The Flash.” To sweeten the offer, Zaslav also allowed Gunn and Safran to be relatively autonomous, reporting directly to him, whereas Skydance wanted the DC leadership to be under Skydance Motion Picture Group chiefs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein.

Skydance has also been stunned by the financial picture of Warner Bros.’ film unit since taking over. The studio has suffered a devastating wave of flops this year, losing hundreds of millions on a slate that included bombs such as “Digger,” “The Bride!,” and last weekend’s “The Cat in the Hat.” One insider put the estimated losses at nearing $1 billion. Of course, most of those films were greenlit under Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy, who were let go as soon as David Ellison got the keys to the Warner lot, and have nothing to do with Gunn or Safran. But it does put pressure on Skydance to turn things around and improve the film division’s margins, fast. On an earnings call this week, Ellison acknowledged the film division faces “headwinds” and “has underperformed this year.” He went on to pledge to “apply the same playbook we did at Paramount: greenlighting more selectively.”

Safran remains widely respected on the lot for his stewardship of DC, and is praised for trying to keep budgets in line and for cleaning up the company’s byzantine production practices so that its films, shows, and comic books had a unifying creative voice. Gunn, though a gifted filmmaker, had a harder time adjusting to life in the c-suite, something he admitted to this week in a lengthy post on X. “What only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least,” Gunn wrote. “I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.” He closed by saying that he was excited to return to working purely as a creator.

Gunn’s habit of engaging with fans directly on social media raised eyebrows at Warner Bros. and, later, at Skydance. But it cut both ways, with Gunn often using his vast following to promote upcoming projects and to engage more directly with fans in a way that inspired loyalty. Insiders also credit Safran and Gunn with not only reinvigorating Superman on screen, but also backing critically acclaimed shows such as “Lanterns” and “Peacemaker.” And the pair handled a delicate situation with the production of “The Batman: Part II,” which was delayed because of personal issues involving its writer and director Matt Reeves, a situation that ultimately required Steven Soderbergh to step in to finish the sequel under Reeves’ guidance. It is expected to wrap production in the next few weeks.

Insiders also note that Gunn and Safran didn’t have a chance to fully realize their vision of making superhero films featuring a wider variety of characters across a greater diversity of genres made for a broader range of budgets. Gunn was already plotting his next move even as he edited “Man of Tomorrow,” which features a team-up of Lex Luthor and Superman. He had outlined a third “Superman” film and was working on a “Justice League” and a “Batman” film, either one of which was expected to be his next project.

In Hollywood, however, timing is everything. And Gunn and Safran had the misfortune of trying to build their own MCU just as comic book movies were declining in popularity. Will Latcham have more success? He’s widely liked and boasts ties to the Christian community that could broaden DC’s core audience. But he also doesn’t come with the kind of pedigree and profile that Gunn did.

As for DC’s fans, they are bracing for yet another reboot having seen the comic book brand they love go through three different regimes over the last decade. Will Latcham provide the kind of consistency the company so desperately needs, or will he be just the latest in a long line of executives asked to pull off a miracle without being granted much of a runway?

entry.title: ‘Paper Tiger’ Review: Adam Driver Gives a Career-Best Performance in James Gray’s Devastating Tragedy
entry.summary: Like all of James Gray's best films, "Paper Tiger" is both sweepingly mythic and hauntingly personal all at once.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 16, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release the film in theaters Friday, November 13.]

It’s the final weekend of summer in 1986, upwardly aspirant Jewish families across Queens are still crowding around country club pools to make sure they get their annual money’s worth, and — in a little less than two months — the Mets are going to win the World Series for what might be the last time in team history. But nebbishy engineer Irwin Pearl (Miles Teller) doesn’t know that yet. He doesn’t know that this is his golden age. He doesn’t know that this is as good as it’s ever going to get. 

Related Stories
Kate Berlant and John Early to Host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards
‘Iron Boy’ Trailer: Beloved Animated Feature Oscar Contender Throws a Whole Watercolor World Out of Whack

What Irwin knows is that greed is good. That the income gap is widening at an unprecedented rate, that economic mobility is slowing to a crawl, and that his giant older brother Gary (Adam Driver) — a divorced ex-police officer who swans around the city like a majestic bird in a blue Mercedes — has started to make him feel even smaller than usual. What Irwin knows is that his mother-in-law wants him to move the family to Great Neck, that the older of his two bickering teenage sons wants an expensive party for his 18th birthday, and that his beautiful wife Hester (Scarlett Johansson) wants fewer things to worry about. Irwin isn’t the overly ambitious sort, but a man can only live in the suburbs of Mt. Olympus for so long before it starts to feel like the gods are taunting him to claim a small piece of it for himself.

And so the stage is set for James Gray’s deft and devastating “Paper Tiger,” a Jewish-American tragedy in a teapot that — like all of the writer/director’s best films — is both sweepingly mythic and hauntingly personal all at once. That double effect, once a magic trick that Gray’s movies would manage to pull off by the time they ended, has since become the de facto starting condition of his singular auto-cinema, which continues to pick at his formative wounds by processing them through the classics. 

As indebted to Aeschylus as “Ad Astra” was to Joseph Campbell, or “The Lost City of Z” was to Henri Rousseau, “Paper Tiger” begins with a telling quote from the ancient playwright’s most famous text: “Let there be wealth without tears; enough for the wise man who will ask no further.” Even more telling, however, is the opening shot that follows, which surveys the same reedy marshland — or at least one identical to it — from the end of “We Own the Night.” It’s no surprise that a project first conceived as a direct sequel to 2022’s “Armageddon Time” should point back to Gray’s previous work, but never before has it been so clear, so fast, that he’s trying to process his own, highly specific experience by assimilating it into the curriculum that first taught him how to make sense of the world. The more acutely self-referential his films get, the more broadly they speak to the soft and immortal agony that propels their characters forward. 

It’s an agony that goes by many (sur)names, but is colloquially referred to as “family.” “Paper Tiger” is many things, chief among them a textbook parable about the American Dream, a breathless thriller about a working-class schmuck who gets mixed up with the Russian mafiya, and a pleasantly open question about why Miles Teller has rededicated his career to cosplaying as “Lost in America”-era Albert Brooks (to my mind, a canny, convincing way of aging up the nonconformist spunk that first defined his screen image in the days of “Whiplash” and “The Spectacular Now”). But, at its most nuclear level, “Paper Tiger” is — to an even more explicit degree than “Little Odessa,” “The Yards,” and any of the other James Gray movies that it hungrily mulches into something all its own — a remarkably knowing and perceptive film about how family is, and has always been, the ultimate devil’s bargain. Our greatest strength and our heaviest cross to bear. The reason our most dangerous risks can seem worth taking, and the most valuable thing we risk by taking them. 

Irwin gives “Paper Tiger” its shape, but it’s how Gary navigates those dilemmas that gives the film its soul. Heartbreakingly portrayed by Adam Driver in a career-best performance that stretches across flash, menace, and pure sincerity like a foot stepping down on a bed of nails without drawing blood, Gary is a vintage ’80s showboat who only knows how to show affection by offering to share in his apparent success. He strides into Irwin and Hester’s living room — after months of radio silence — with the razzle dazzle of a local celebrity and a fully catered feast from Peter Luger’s Steak House in tow for good measure. Irwin’s sons marvel at the gun their uncle still keeps holstered around his ankle (cool!), and his wide-eyed wife looks across the kitchen table and imagines what her life might have been like had she held out for the shinier Pearl. 

At least, that’s what Irwin seems to imagine that his wife is imagining, though he’d sooner let such fears fester inside of him for the rest of his natural life than to speak them aloud. For all of the character’s frustrated aspirations for a better life, Teller endows him with the wizened humility of a second-generation Jewish immigrant who knows that it would be gauche to forsake what his late father-in-law — tempting to picture as Anthony Hopkins for continuity’s sake — sacrificed to make possible for their family. Irwin might even be smart enough to recognize that his brother is an empty promise in a tailored suit, but, in a less literal expression of the double vision that will soon cause his wife to crash her car into a tree, being smart isn’t the same as seeing things clearly.

Whatever the case, Irwin is powerless to resist his brother’s sales pitch when Gary lures him into the basement to reveal the reason purpose of his visit: An ambitious new business venture is seeping its way into the Gowanus Canal, and it could use a sharp engineer to help facilitate their plans for the waterway. Still connected to the gills after getting rich in the private sector, Gary doesn’t tell his naive kid brother that said venture is the Russian mob, but the beauty of it is that he doesn’t have to. It can just be another one of the many different things that Irwin doesn’t know. He’ll go down there, sketch a few diagrams for some bald and scary men straight out of central casting, and take home a healthy paycheck to his family (“Paper Tiger” won’t score any points for bucking mafia stereotypes, as Gray plays up their ruthlessness in order to stress how far Irwin is out of his depth). 

The only problem is that Irwin takes the job as seriously as he would any other, and — to his profound regret — takes his two sons to go scope out the canal one night, where they see the Russians illegally dumping their waste into the water. The Russians don’t like that. They don’t know what he’s doing there. And, in the aftermath of a stomach-churning stick-up that twisted my guts with the queasy horror of a repressed memory, Gary is given a week to make the problem go away. Spoiler alert: Appeasing the leader of an organized crime ring isn’t as simple as cutting a check, and wouldn’t be even if Gary had access to $125,000. 

It doesn’t take long for things to spiral out of control from there, as Irwin and his boys soon find themselves in the crosshairs of a turf war they are comically ill-prepared to survive, while Hester — kept in the dark for her own protection — is thrust into a different crucible that she chooses to keep secret from her husband for similar reasons. (Despite being heavily affected by period drag, Johansson’s performance is too limpid to be mistaken for caricature, growing more hollowed out and heartsick with every scene until it assumes the same void-like power that Brad Pitt once found in the farthest reaches of outer space.) Plotted with a fatalistic velocity that would make Aeschylus proud, Gray’s script corkscrews towards ruin at a sickening pace, its slick road to hell paved with a well-textured mixture of imperfect intentions. 

For all of the red meat that “Paper Tiger” gets to chew off the bone, this is still a small and maybe slightly underfunded movie, its outsized impact only made possible because of the micro-details that Gray traces within and between his characters. And I’m not talking about the assortment of beepers and TaB cans, or the load-bearing shots of ’80s New York, which are all Joaquín Baca-Asay’s 35mm cinematography needs to complete the illusion of time travel. While the film is buttressed by a handful of exquisite setpieces (including a nightmarish home invasion sequence that transposes the film’s title into a piece of shadowplay, and a climactic shoutout that binds it even closer to the rest of Gray’s body of work), it’s ultimately fueled by the atomic frictions inside Driver’s performance. 

To that point, the real tragedy of “Paper Tiger” isn’t that messing with the mob tears these brothers apart, but rather that it brings them together. There’s not a lot of time for fun and games, but it’s never lost on Gray that this is the most time Gary and Irwin have spent with each other in years — maybe even since they were kids. “We’ve never played in the dirt,” Gary tells Irwin as he lies to his brother about how everything  about the Gowanus deal is above board. But they’re playing together now. The worse things get, the more they expose the extraordinary bond that allowed things to get so fucked up in the first place (a dynamic that becomes all the more wrenching because of how Gray transposes it onto Irwin’s sons). The worse things get, the more this movie sympathizes with Gary and Irwin for their parts in it. 

It’s not that Gary is trying to do something nice for his brother, or that he’s shamelessly using Irwin to broker a lucrative deal with the Russians, but rather that everything that happens after that fateful offer stems from an inextricable braid of love and leverage. Gray is no stranger to saga about fraternal strains, but never has he so forcefully tugged at the ties that bind, or more sensitively observed how they can suffocate an entire family when a certain force pulls on them hard enough. 

“Paper Tiger” is a story about a household gripped by a self-inflicted event that chokes the life out of its lungs, and precious few films have better conveyed what it feels like when the oxygen gets sucked out of a home without any hope of coming back. “We already had everything,” Irwin will eventually mutter under his breath. The deepest cut of this unshakeable tragedy is that, for the very first time, it leaves him begging for more. 

Grade: A

“Paper Tiger” premiered in Competition at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. NEON will release it in theaters later this year.

entry.title: Kate Berlant and John Early to Host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards
entry.summary: Comedians Kate Berlant and John Early will host the 42nd annual Film Independent Spirit Awards at the Hollywood Palladium on Saturday, March 6, 2027.
entry.content:
The Film Independent Spirit Awards are returning to the Hollywood Palladium with a new pair of hosts in tow.

Film Independent, the nonprofit organization dedicated to championing independent storytelling and supporting artists, announced on Wednesday, December 10 that “Maddie’s Secret” stars Kate Berlant and John Early will co-host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards.

The acclaimed comedians, actors and longtime creative collaborators, who have written and/or starred together in other projects like Emmy-nominated variety special “Would It Kill You to Laugh?,” and cult comedy series “Search Party” will bring their comedic sensibilities to the 42nd annual Spirit Awards. The celebration of the best in independent film and television takes place Saturday, March 6, 2027 in Los Angeles, California.

Related Stories
Jeremy O. Harris EPs ‘American Theater,’ About a Canceled MAGA Theater Director’s Bizarre Attempted Comeback — Watch the Trailer
‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: David Leitch’s Fun and Poppy YouTube Heist Movie Almost Gets Away with It

“If there’s one thing we don’t need, it’s another predictable awards show,” said Juan Devis, President of Film Independent, as part of the announcement. “Kate and John are two of the funniest, strangest and most brilliantly unpredictable performers working today. They embody everything we love about independent storytelling: originality, fearlessness and a healthy disregard for convention. We’re excited to shake things up, break a few rules and have some fun along the way.”

“We’ve always been obsessed with awards shows, and we’re so honored we get to host the coolest one,” the hosts said in a joint statement. “Tune in to see if we choke under pressure!”

Nominations will be announced on Wednesday, December 2. The 2027 ceremony will introduce the Best International First Feature and Digital Creator Award categories, said to further expand the Spirit Awards’ recognition of bold, original storytelling across platforms and around the world.

In other recent developments, acclaimed filmmaker Roman Coppola will contribute to the ceremony in his new creative consultant role. The Nominee Brunch, an annual highlight honoring all nominees and featuring the presentation of the Emerging Filmmaker Awards, will take place on Saturday, January 9, 2027 at The London West Hollywood.

Berlant and Early join a roster of past Spirit Awards hosts that includes Ego Nwodim, Aidy Bryant, Hasan Minhaj, Megan Mullally and Nick Offerman, Aubrey Plaza, Nick Kroll and John Mulaney, Kate McKinnon and Kumail Nanjiani, Fred Armisen and Kristen Bell, Andy Samberg, and John Waters.

entry.title: ‘Iron Boy’ Trailer: Beloved Animated Feature Oscar Contender Throws a Whole Watercolor World Out of Whack
entry.summary: Watch the trailer for director Louis Clichy's beautifully off-balance coming-of-age story 'Iron Boy,' a Best Animated Feature Oscar contender.
entry.content:
Maybe you’re the kind of person who thinks about the first 10 minutes of “Up” from time to time, and wishes there was a film out there that would emotionally break you like that again. Maybe you long for less-processed-looking Minionesque animation and more painterly, natural worlds that find as much beauty in negative space as in color. Maybe it’s been a minute since “Flow,” and you would like a protagonist to hang out with another very good animated dog.

If your answer to any of the above is “yes,” then IndieWire has good news for you. The Annecy and Cannes Un Certain Regard Special Jury Prize-winning film “Iron Boy” is coming to U.S. theaters for a one-week awards-qualifying run in December, then launching in select cities on January 22, 2027. Writer/director Louis Clichy is a veteran of Pixar’s most undefeated run of films, including “Wall-E” and “Up,” as well as two fantastical “Asterix” adventures in France. With “Iron Boy,” he shows how big a seemingly small story can feel.

Related Stories
Kate Berlant and John Early to Host the 2027 Film Independent Spirit Awards
Jeremy O. Harris EPs ‘American Theater,’ About a Canceled MAGA Theater Director’s Bizarre Attempted Comeback — Watch the Trailer

Young farmboy Christophe starts tilting his head unintentionally, which eventually leads to a scoliosis diagnosis and an iron corset he has to wear everywhere. But, of course, his spine is far from the only thing out of alignment in Christophe’s life — straightening those emotions and ambitions out, discovering who he wants to be, is the real journey. But it’s one that occasionally turns its entire watercolor world sideways like the most beautiful magical realist snowglobe you’ve ever seen.

It’s one that, as Rafael Motomayor said in IndieWire’s review, “makes ‘Iron Boy’ stand out even amongst European animated films. The film employs mostly non-professional voice actors, including Clinchy’s own son (who plays Christophe), and the director would often record the lines on location, to give the performances a less constructed sound than if they were done in the clear confines of a studio. It makes the story feel quasi-documentary in its approach, an intimate and deeply personal story of a boy searching for more than what life has offered him, restrained by a physical affliction that nevertheless allows him to live an extraordinary life.”

entry.title: Jeremy O. Harris EPs ‘American Theater,’ About a Canceled MAGA Theater Director’s Bizarre Attempted Comeback — Watch the Trailer
entry.summary: Jeremy O. Harris tells IndieWire about 'American Theater,' a documentary that follows a canceled MAGA theater director's attempted comeback.
entry.content:
Can a conservative “canceled” theater director rise from the ashes of his own ruination — and in this climate? That’s one of the questions top of mind for filmmakers Nicholas Clark and Dylan Frederick, whose provocative, Christopher Guest-style nonfiction film “American Theater” (except it’s a docu-, not mockumentary) is rolling out in select theaters now. A Slamdance Grand Jury Prize winner for documentary in 2025, the film is also executive-produced by Jeremy O. Harris.

“American Theater” follows Brian Clowdus — openly gay, conservative, and formerly of the Serenbe Playhouse in Georgia, who was taken down in 2019 over allegations of racism, misconduct, unsafe working conditions, and a gamut of other accusations. Clark and Frederick follow Clowdus, now a MAGA Republican, and a troupe of other conservative actors to an abandoned cabin in middle-of-nowhere Georgia where Clowdus plots the ultimate revenge: a community musical theater retelling of, of course, the 1692 Salem witch trials, riffing on Arthur Miller’s “The Crucible” (which, published in 1953, isn’t yet in the public domain).

Related Stories
Fan Edits Are Legal with Moonbeem, Distribution Network Hosts Approved Clips from Filmmakers
‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: David Leitch’s Fun and Poppy YouTube Heist Movie Almost Gets Away with It

“This film was about a really fucked-up figure and a person with really fucked-up politics,” Harris told IndieWire over the phone from Copenhagen, where the Tony nominee is rehearsing a new play. “When you have unwelcoming and fucked-up politics, or a person who has unwelcoming, fucked-up politics at the center of the art you’re making, it can feel like potentially you’re endorsing their politics or celebrating them, especially because we don’t live in times that are deeply discursive or critical. At least having my name in the headline should be an invitation to certain people that maybe would’ve been like, ‘I’m not watching that,’ that maybe this is something for them.”

In taking on someone who was once a formidable presence in the Southern regional theater space, Harris said the filmmakers saw “this opportunity to embed themselves in the company for his comeback show. They realized there was a chance to look at the type of fringe character that utilized MAGA for the grifting machine that it is. MAGA is a magnet for a lot of displaced people, and theater has so many displaced people. Even thinking about the fact that one of the most famous people that stormed the Capitol was in the regional production of ‘Jesus Christ Superstar’ meant that there were ways in which the theater community wasn’t looking at some of the foxes among the lambs in our own community. This gave them the opportunity to be those foxes, or not even foxes, but to be flies on the wall of this maker who was exploiting a lot of displaced people.”

A recent Cobble Hill Cinemas screening of “American Theater” was moderated by journalist Ludwig Hurtado. Next up, the film will be available to rent on the Letterboxd Video Store, so locally driven screenings also aim to bring audiences to that platform.

“One of the things that’s very sad to me is that amongst the distributors, the ones that one would think have the most bandwidth and power to really uplift these microbudget filmmakers who are truly keeping the torch burning for that independent American brio that put American independent cinema on the map and right next to so many other stalwarts of world cinema, a lot of them are being, I think, more cautious about who they’re distributing,” Harris said. “Distribution costs are so large right now that I think that they don’t really know what to do with movies so small. And so Letterboxd has become this really great outlet because there’s such a vibrant community there who are just excited to see films and excited to learn that filmmakers who maybe are in circumstances similar to their own as movie watchers are making films.”

In a separate statement, Frederick said, “The film takes place in 2021, when Trump was facing the possibility of spending the rest of his life in prison, his political future was uncertain, and conservatives were batching DeSantis ‘24 tank tops. Democrats just had the best night of their lives in the midterms, and MAGA folks may find themselves at a low point, but it’s useful to remember that we’ve actually been here before.”

Clark added, “There was a moment when many people assumed the Trump era had come to an end. ‘American Theater’ tells a story of the Trump supporters during that time who were dedicated to figuring out what would come next. In this instance, their idea was an allegorical cancel culture musical about the Salem witch trials. It did not go anywhere near as planned, and our movie tells that story. But ultimately, everything that has happened to us as a nation ever since has only recontextualized what we saw within this brief moment in time.”
